38 When -particles are directed at gold leaf:
1
almost all -particles pass through without deflection
2
a few -particles are deviated through large angles.
What are the reasons for these effects?
1
2
A
most -particles have enough energy
to pass right through the gold leaf
gold is very dense so a few low
energy -particles bounce back
from the gold surface
B
most -particles miss all gold atoms
a few -particles bounce off gold atoms
C
the gold nucleus is very small
so most -particles miss all nuclei
occasionally the path of an
-particle is close to a nucleus
D
occasionally an -particle
experiences many small
deflections in the same direction
the positive charge in an
atom is not concentrated
enough to deflect an -particle

hints: Notice the contrast in the stem: observation 1 is almost all $\alpha$-particles undeflected, while observation 2 is a few deviated through large angles by the gold leaf.
Remember both the $\alpha$-particle and the gold nucleus have positive charge, so the deflecting force is electrostatic repulsion that grows very strong only at very small separation.
Ask which model gives both results: a tiny concentrated nucleus that most particles miss but a close particle feels strongly, versus spread-out charge or bouncing off whole atoms.
walkthrough: Recall the Rutherford $\alpha$-scattering experiment: positively charged $\alpha$-particles are fired at thin gold leaf and most go straight through.

Observation 1 means the atom is mostly empty space. The positive charge and mass occupy a nucleus about $10^{-14} \text{ m}$ across, far smaller than the atom, so most $\alpha$-particles never come near a nucleus.

Observation 2 means a strong repulsive force acts rarely. Only an $\alpha$-particle with a direct close approach to a small, concentrated positive nucleus experiences a large electrostatic force and scatters through a large angle.

Options A and B fail because the effect does not depend on some $\alpha$-particles having more energy or on missing whole gold atoms. Option D describes the old spread-out charge model, which can only give small deflections.
Together, a very small nucleus explains both almost all missing and rare large deflections. This is option C

A.explanation: All $\alpha$-particles have similar high energy and pass through because the atom is mostly empty space, not because of excess energy. Large-angle scattering is electrostatic repulsion by a nucleus, not low-energy particles bouncing off a dense surface.

B.explanation: An $\alpha$-particle passes through thousands of gold atoms in the leaf, so it cannot miss all atoms. What it usually misses is the tiny nucleus at the centre of each atom.

C.explanation: Most $\alpha$-particles pass far from any tiny nucleus so feel negligible repulsion. A rare close approach to a small, highly charged nucleus gives a large electrostatic deflection.

D.explanation: The plum-pudding idea of spread-out positive charge predicts only small deflections, never large angles. Many small deflections in the same direction cannot add up to back-scattering.
